analysis.one_liner: Blocks OSHA from issuing or enforcing its first-ever national workplace heat-safety standard.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 12 Republican cosponsors, sits in the Senate labor committee with no action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: OSHA proposed a rule in 2024 requiring employers to give workers water, shade, rest breaks, and heat-safety plans when temperatures get dangerous [S2]. This bill would forbid the Labor Department from finalizing, carrying out, or enforcing that rule — or anything like it — so no federal heat-safety standard could take effect [S2]. The bill has gone no further than being sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing, delivery, land-clearing, and food processing — would avoid the costs of writing heat-safety plans, providing water, shade, and rest breaks, and following acclimatization rules for new workers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing OSHA's proposed 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' standard, or any substantially similar standard, permanently [S2].
The bill's findings argue the proposed rule is overly prescriptive and burdensome to businesses, citing requirements like high-heat triggers, rest-break protocols, and written safety plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Outdoor and hot-indoor workers — farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers — would continue to face heat illness and heat deaths with no federal right to water, shade, rest breaks, or heat-safety planning [S2].

drawbacks.text: Heat is a leading weather-related killer of U.S. workers; blocking the standard leaves farm, construction, and warehouse workers with no federal heat-safety protections, a cost an honest supporter must weigh against compliance burdens [S2].

The ban covers 'any substantially similar standard,' which would prevent OSHA from ever issuing a narrower, more flexible heat rule than the 2024 proposal — the bill rules out any federal heat standard, not just the specific one [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is avoiding compliance costs that its own findings call burdensome for businesses [S2]. The cost is that workers in hot jobs get no federal protection from a recognized occupational hazard; the bill forecloses not just this rule but any version of it [S2].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote [S1][S4].

narrative.text: OSHA published the proposed 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' standard in the Federal Register on August 30, 2024 [S2].
Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on April 29, 2026, joined by eight original cosponsors — Risch, Tuberville, Crapo, Budd, Daines, Sheehy, Cornyn, and Tillis — all Republicans [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; no further action is recorded [S4].
Twelve senators, all Republicans, have cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one's position has changed; the rule is blocked only on paper, and employers in hot industries gain nothing until the bill moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, so far unaffected — the bill has stalled

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors are Republicans and no Democrat has signed on; there have been no votes, so the chamber's actual split is unknown [S3].

industries.industry: Agriculture, construction, warehousing, and delivery employers
industries.note: The bill spares these employers the costs of heat-safety plans, water, shade, and mandated rest breaks [S2]. The burden avoided comes out of protections for their own workers, whose interest runs opposite to theirs.
The bill would permanently stop OSHA from issuing any national heat standard, narrowing the government's ability to regulate a leading workplace hazard [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one committee referral and no hearings or markups scheduled; most one-sponsor committee referrals never reach the floor, and even if it cleared the Senate HELP Committee it would need 60 votes to advance past a filibuster, which its all-Republican cosponsor list does not suggest [S1][S4][S3].
